title: Is a Dubrovnik to Korčula Day Trip Worth It? 2027
metaDescription: Honest verdict on a Dubrovnik to Korčula day trip in 2027: ferry times, costs, what you can see in a day, and who should skip it.
content:
## Is the Dubrovnik to Korčula day trip worth it?

It is worth it for travellers who want a compact medieval town, a quiet lunch and a short walk, and who will be in Dubrovnik in summer. It is not worth it for those who prioritise beaches, hiking or nightlife. The reason is simple: about 4 hours of the day go to sailing, and the Old Town can be seen in 2 to 3 hours.

## Time and cost breakdown

The ferry from Dubrovnik to Korčula Town takes about 1h 55m to 2h 10m. Fares start around €10 on some TP Line and Krilo sailings and reach about €30 for adults on the Krilo Naranča catamaran, which runs daily in the main season (roughly mid-May to mid-October) and calls at Mljet (Pomena) on the way. Most services are passenger-only, with 3 to 7 sailings a day depending on the season.

A realistic budget for one person:

- Return ferry: €20–€60
- Lunch in the Old Town: €15–€30
- Tower, museum or church entries: €6–€20
- Total: about €45–€110

The catch is timing. Morning departures from Dubrovnik leave around 07:00–08:00 in peak season, and the last sailing back is mid-afternoon. Check the return time before you book the outbound. Some days the last boat leaves Korčula well before dinner, which cuts your time on the island to about 4 hours.

## What you can see in 4–5 hours

Korčula Old Town sits on a small oval peninsula with a herringbone street plan, designed so that streets break the wind. It can be crossed on foot in a few minutes. A loop covers:

- St. Mark's Cathedral and its square
- The Town Tower and the walls
- The Marco Polo house claim (the birthplace is disputed, and the house is mostly a viewing tower)
- The waterfront promenade toward Banje beach

That is 1 to 1.5 hours at a normal pace. The rest of the day goes to lunch, a swim and the ferry queue.

## Honest verdict

The Marco Polo angle is overrated. The "birthplace" is contested, and paying to climb the house is the weakest use of your money in town. Spend it on a long lunch and a swim instead. The town's real appeal is the walk along the walls at golden hour, and a day trip often misses that because the boat leaves early.

For a better version of the same day, consider an organised tour that adds a Pelješac wine stop, or stay one night. A night in the Old Town after the day-trippers leave is the stronger experience.

## Who should skip it

- **Beach-focused travellers.** The pebbly town beaches are small. Lumbarda's sandy beaches, about 6 km away, need a bus or taxi and extra time.
- **Anyone visiting November to March.** Many restaurants and shops close, and sailings are fewer.
- **Travellers who get seasick.** Catamaran crossings in strong bura or jugo winds can be rough, and cancellations occur.
- **Families with small children.** Two hours each way is a long ride for a short visit.
- **People with only one day in Dubrovnik.** Spend it in Dubrovnik and the Elaphiti Islands instead.

## Who should do it

- Travellers already based in Dubrovnik for 3 or more days
- Wine drinkers (Pošip and Plavac Mali are local)
- Photographers and history fans who like small walled towns
- Visitors who want an easy, low-effort day without driving

## Local tips

- Book the earliest outbound and the latest return. This is the best way to protect your 5 hours on the island.
- Have lunch away from the main square, in side streets or just outside the walls. Prices drop noticeably.
- Swim at Banje beach, a 10-minute walk from the Old Town, instead of paying for a boat taxi.
- Carry your ID or passport. Operators may ask for it at boarding.
- Foot passenger tickets sell out on peak July and August days. Book a few days ahead.

## Alternatives

The Dubrovnik to Mljet crossing takes about 75 minutes and costs around €25 on the Krilo service, and it is a better choice for nature lovers. A Pelješac peninsula wine tour by road is cheaper and has no seasickness risk.

faq.question: How long is the ferry from Dubrovnik to Korčula?
faq.answer: The fastest ferries take about 1 hour 55 minutes, and the average crossing is around 2 hours. Services that stop at Mljet take longer.

faq.question: How much does a day trip from Dubrovnik to Korčula cost?
faq.answer: Expect about €45–€110 per person including a return ferry (€20–€60), lunch and a small entry fee. Organised tours cost more, roughly €80–€130.

faq.question: Is one day enough for Korčula?
faq.answer: One day covers the Old Town, but not the beaches, Lumbarda or the wine villages. Travellers with 2 days or a night on the island get much more out of the visit.

faq.question: When is the best time for a Korčula day trip?
faq.answer: June and September offer the best balance of full ferry schedules, open restaurants and manageable crowds. July and August have the most sailings but also the highest prices and busiest boats.

quickAnswer: A day trip from Dubrovnik to Korčula Town is worth it only in summer, and only if you take a morning ferry back. The crossing takes about 2 hours each way and costs roughly €20–60 return. That leaves 4–5 hours on the island. Skip it in shoulder season or if you want beaches.
